# Book index: Werner's 101 Free Repairs

- **Channel:** Werner Finkbeiner. **Author:** Werner Finkbeiner (as printed on the title page and in the running header of every repair page).
- **Exact printed title** (used in CTA markers): Werner's 101 Free Repairs. The title page adds the subtitle "The German Way to Fix Anything for Free".
- **What's in it:** twelve chapters and 101 numbered repairs. Chapter 1 frames the book (the ninety-five-dollar garbage-disposal call, the book's thesis, the four named ideas, how to use the book); chapters 2 to 11 hold the repairs; chapter 12 is where to start. Each repair page carries "The Problem", "The Old Way", "What You Need", "When to Stop" and "Money Saved" (from chapter 3 on, several repairs drop the "The Problem" label but keep the other four).
- **Source:** the text the operator pasted into the chat on 2026-10-27 (the whole book, from the title page to page 511). The PDF itself (werner's_101_free_repairs_ebook.pdf, 115 MB, in the channel's 3_EBOOKS folder in Drive) can't be read by the Drive tools: Drive returns no text for it and it is over the 10 MB download limit.
- **Page numbers:** the pasted text carries one page number at the foot of each page, 3 to 511. The pages below are those numbers: a repair's page is the page its title starts on. They are close to, but not checked against, a PDF reader's page count.
- **What this file holds:** the chapter page map, every repair's title, page and Money Saved figure, the book's own first-person stories (which never go in a script), and the facts a CTA may state. **The full text is not stored here** (the paste was the only copy that could be read); the operator's paste in the chat of 2026-10-27 is the record. Ask for a text export if the full text is ever needed in the library.
- **Use:** for the book match (which repair and chapter cover a video's topic) and the facts a CTA may state. It supplies no facts, steps or numbers to the script itself.

## Facts a CTA may state

- Twelve chapters, one hundred and one numbered repairs; the subtitle "The German Way to Fix Anything for Free".
- Every repair has the same parts: The Problem, The Old Way, What You Need, When to Stop, Money Saved.
- The four ideas that run through it by name: the Prevention-First Principle, the Scrap-Not-Spend Rule, the One-Tool, One-Job Method, and the Smell-and-See Test.
- Who it's for (p. 9): "anyone who owns or rents a home and would rather spend twenty minutes fixing something than two hundred dollars explaining it to someone else"; it is not for "a full renovation, rewiring a panel, or replacing a roof", and "will tell you plainly when you've reached one".
- Chapter 12's starter week (p. 510): five first repairs, 12 (the squeaky hinge), 54 (the flapper), 32 (the picture-hook hole), 62 (the loose cabinet hinge) and 82 (the tripped breaker).
- A repair's Money Saved figure, as the table below gives it. Never the page count, price, file format or any bonus (not in the book).

## Never in a script: the book's own first-person stories

The book is written in a first-person voice whose history doesn't match Werner's profile (he grew up in Germany; the book's narrator grew up in a house with "humid Texas summer[s]"). The claims policy keeps all of it out of every script, and his profile's scanner bans the names. For the record:

| Page | What the book says |
|---|---|
| 3 | "I once paid a repair technician ninety-five dollars to turn an Allen wrench." (the garbage disposal) |
| 7, 11, 15, 70, 330, 359, 394-395, 404, 457, 474, 507, 511 | his mother: "My mother, Bertha, never owned a toolbox…"; "Bertha used to say a house complains in whispers before it ever screams"; "The back door of the house I grew up in… every humid Texas summer" (p. 70); Bertha's coffee can (p. 457); "she had a mother who showed her" (p. 511) |
| 35, 95, 137-138, 177, 244-245, 279, 319-322, 403-406, 409, 428, 471 | a neighbour, Marcus: the downspout, the candle-stub drawer, the walking washer, the hallway patch, the bacon grease, a water bill "close to $100 a month when it had run closer to $55-$65", the toothpicks, the mouse, the GFCI, the kitchen overload; on p. 471 the book calls the narrator "Werner" in the third person |
| 83, 121, 168, 216, 269, 311, 359, 410, 507 | the narrator's own mistakes: over-planing a hallway door, a strap that split a copper joint "in the first house I owned outright", a cracked spackle patch, a split trap, a cracked faucet handle cap, a split cabinet panel, a dryer-vent rag a mouse chewed through, a garage GFCI, a fourteen-attachment drill kit |

The book never mentions Germany beyond its subtitle, and never mentions a mentor, a father or a trade.
